storm.summary_layperson: A steady, soaking rain with some heavier bursts continues this evening, but there is no thunderstorm fuel in the air, and the cove will get the same wet, breezy weather as the surrounding towns — the Sound is not helping or hurting tonight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer tonight: the Sound (64°F) is about 7°F warmer than the air at 4 PM and stays 5–6°F warmer through 7 PM, so there is no cool, stable layer over the water to weaken the rain.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: a broad shield of rain covers the area. The 3:49 PM radar scan showed moderate-to-heavy pockets all around the cove — the nearest about 9–13 miles north and north-northeast, more 16–22 miles to the northwest and west — with a peak intensity that counts as heavy rain, not hail or severe weather. Every nearby station has measured rain in the last hour (roughly 0.1–0.2 inch), and Riverside Yacht Club was reporting light rain at 4 PM. The National Weather Service calls for rain at 100% with another half to three-quarters of an inch, and there are no alerts in effect.

Why the risk reads moderate, not low: heavier rain pockets are close by, which is what sets the level. But this is a rain event, not a thunderstorm event. The atmosphere has zero storm fuel (the model shows no instability at all through 7 PM), so although the winds aloft are strong and change sharply with height — about 50–65 kt of difference between the surface and 6 km — there is nothing for them to organize into thunderstorms. The NWS forecast discussion does not mention thunder until Tuesday night.

Local effect — none tonight: the cove's usual protection comes from cool Sound water chilling the air above it into a stable layer that starves incoming storms. That needs the air to be at least about 5°F warmer than the water. Tonight it is the other way around: the Sound is 64°F and the air is 57°F, so the water is about 7°F warmer than the air at 4 PM, and still 5–6°F warmer through 7 PM. There is no protective layer now and none will form this evening. There is also no sea breeze — the wind is a steady easterly driven by the larger weather pattern.

Most likely outcome for the cove: the same as everywhere nearby — periods of rain, at times briefly heavy, with a raw east wind around 15 kt and stronger gusts on exposed shoreline (one Old Greenwich waterfront station gusted to 28 kt just before 4 PM). The rain as a whole is drifting northeast at about 21 kt. The pockets to the north are moving away, but more rain 20 miles to the west and west-southwest is lined up to move through over the next hour or so. No single approaching storm cell is being tracked, so no arrival time is given.

What would change the call: any sign of instability appearing ahead of the rain, a lightning report upstream, or an NWS statement for flooding or wind. None of those is indicated right now.

wind.tactics_blurb: A steady 14–17 kt easterly on the open Sound, but Greenwich Point blocks much of it inside the cove, where it arrives lighter, bent toward the southeast, and in puffs and holes. Stay in the middle of the course and sail to the pressure rather than committing to a side; the wind does not die at sunset.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of wind day: a moderate gradient wind — the breeze is driven by the large-scale weather pattern, with no sea breeze in play. A sea breeze needs the land air to be at least 5°F warmer than the Sound; today the air is about 7°F colder than the 64°F water, under solid cloud and rain. The well-sited airport anemometers average about 9 kt from the east, with Bridgeport at 14 kt, and the model has it building.

Through the window: the model has east at 14 kt at 5 PM, peaking near 17 kt from the east-northeast around 6 PM, then about 15 kt at 7 PM, backing slowly from about 080° to 070° along the way. Because this wind does not depend on the sun, it holds through sunset (6:19 PM) and into the night — no evening collapse. Model data stops at 7 PM in this run, so the 8–10 PM rows carry the 7 PM wind forward, easing only a knot or two, and should be read as estimates.

Model versus the cove: the table shows the open-water breeze. Inside the cove, Riverside Yacht Club was reading southeast (134°) at 8 kt, averaging 9 kt over ten minutes and gusting 19, at 4 PM — about 50° to the right of the model and several knots lighter. That is the Greenwich Point peninsula at work: an easterly is the most sheltered direction for the cove, so the wind arrives weakened and bent around the point. Just outside, an Old Greenwich waterfront station had east 17 kt gusting 28. Expect the start area to feel more like 8–12 kt with sharp gusts than the 14–17 kt in the table. This is a gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day, so the sea-breeze direction correction does not apply.

Where the pressure is and how it shifts: behind the point the wind comes in patches, so no side pays reliably — the east side of the course sits deepest in the wind shadow, and the gusts that get through are large (roughly double the lulls). Stay near the middle, connect the puffs, and tack on the big headers. The slow trend is to the left as the wind backs toward the east-northeast; the further it backs toward northeast, the cleaner and steadier it gets in the cove.

What it feels like: powered-up conditions for dinghies in the gusts, with rain, poor visibility, about 59°F, and darkness after 6:19 PM. On the open Sound it is a solid 15 kt-plus breeze with gusts into the low-to-mid 20s.

data_caveats: HRRR model run only reached 7 PM (forecast hours 5–12 unavailable) — the 8, 9 and 10 PM wind rows are carried forward from the 7 PM value, not model output.
Gust figures are estimates scaled from sustained wind and current station gusts — the model feed has no gust field.
Western Long Island Sound buoy 44040 offline (UConn data server returned an error) — no over-water wind reading; water temperature is from Bridgeport Harbor.
Cove wind differs from the model: Riverside YC reads southeast 8 kt while the model has east 12 kt — the table shows open-water wind, and the cove is sheltered by Greenwich Point.
Storm timing engine tracked only the five nearest rain cells, all moving away; rain upstream to the west was not individually timed.
Radar scan was 3:49 PM, about 12 minutes old at publish time.
